summary: A 1937 CCC-built steel tower and stone residence on Sugarloaf Mountain in Arkansas's Ozark National Forest, unstaffed and showing wear but still standing.

access.note: On Forest Service land; a locked gate blocks the ~1 mi gravel access road, requiring a walk-in of about 500 ft elevation gain. No indication the tower itself is open to climb.

visit.trail_note: Locked gate on the gravel road to the tower; about a mile and 500 ft of elevation gain on foot

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service (Sylamore Ranger District, cooperator)

events.note: 100-ft steel tower with 7x7-ft cab, plus stone residence, privy, and vaulted stone storage cellar, built by a CCC crew
Listed on NRHP September 11, 1995 as Sugarloaf Fire Tower Historic District (ref. 94001615)

evidence.quote: Location Ozark National Forest Stone County, Arkansas Coordinates N 36° 05.017' W 092° 09.866' Elevation 1,089 ft (332 m) Administered by U.S. Forest Service Cooperators Sylamore Ranger District

The mountaintop, located on the Ozark National Forest, is the site of a remarkable group of stone structures constructed by the CCC in 1937 as living accommodations for the 100’ steel lookout tower with 7’x7’ cab.

evidence.supports: NHLR registered August 20, 1996, as US 186, AR 5
evidence.quote:
Registry Numbers
US 186, AR 5 ... Date Registered

evidence.supports: 2012 visit: unstaffed, radio room active, stairs removed
evidence.quote: Locked radio room seems to still be active, other buildings boarded up and first set of stairs has been removed.

evidence.supports: 2023 visit: locked gate, ~1 mi gravel road, ~500 ft climb
evidence.quote: A locked gate blocks the mile-ish long gravel road to get to the tower. A path is visible where trucks have been able to drive around it, but if you're driving a low car or a non 4x4 expect to walk all the way up, as I ended up having to do. There is a ~500 foot elevation gain from this gate to the tower.

evidence.supports: 2023 visit: stairs solid, no glass, antennas outside cab
evidence.quote: Stairs are very solid, mild graffiti scratched into metal, no glass, and antennas that I assumed to be radio equipment are attached to the outside of the cab.

evidence.supports: 2023 visit: stone house broken into, outhouse, cement bunker structure
evidence.quote: There's a very old stone house next to the tower that was previously boarded up, but has been broken into at some point. There is also an old outhouse and a separate, small cement bunker like structure dug into the ground that I thought may have been used for storage at some point.
1937:    A 100-foot steel tower with a 7 x 7 metal cab erected by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

evidence.supports: built 1937 by CCC, included a residence, unusual pairing
evidence.quote: These structures were all built in 1937 by a crew of the Civilian Conservation Corps, and is particularly unusual because the fire watch facility included a residence.

evidence.supports: residence, privy, vaulted stone storage cellar
evidence.quote: alongside which stand a residence, privy, and vaulted stone storage cellar

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NHLR page's prose gives 'October, 1995' for NRHP acceptance, but the NRHP reference itself (via Wikipedia, citing the National Register Information System) gives September 11, 1995; the story and events use the official NRHP date.

notes_for_editor: The NHLR narrative text says NRHP acceptance was 'October, 1995' while the official NRHP reference number's listing date (via Wikipedia/NRIS) is September 11, 1995; I used the official date and noted the discrepancy. Access status recorded as 'unknown' in facts because sources describe a locked gate on the road but say nothing about whether climbing the tower itself is permitted; did not mark it climbable. Did not use any WebSearch calls; three cached/live page reads (NHLR, Central US Lookouts, Wikipedia) were sufficient. Fact-check (2026-10-04): the summit elevation is also given inconsistently across sources -- NHLR says 1,089 ft, Wikipedia says 1,150 ft; the story follows NHLR since that is the only source the elevation sentence cites, but a human may want to reconcile the two.
